rubric: GPT-6 Codex editorial review. Read historical comments and current contexts, identify the mechanism, actor, intervention, and warranted inference, then check against primary source and rendered page. Local readiness 3 means source and context checked. 4 requires author or advisor confirmation. Unmarked passages are unlabeled.

passages.author: Ben and database reviewer
passages.question: Why create SADb?
passages.before: I developed the Sensory Afferent Database (SADb), a curated literature resource for studying sensory feedback in locomotion and posture. It links findings from animal and human studies to afferent classes, sensory afferent pathways, and computational models. Researchers can use these records to compare individual feedback connections or whole neural circuits before implementing a neuromechanical model. This work forms part of the AARL's NeuroNex Communication, Coordination, and Control in Nervous Systems (C3NS) effort.
passages.after: Choosing a sensory connection for a locomotor controller requires more than the name of a receptor. A researcher needs to know which nerve was stimulated, which motor neurons responded, and whether the animal was at rest or moving. Those details are scattered across studies that used different species, preparations, and tasks. I developed the Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) to keep a proposed feedback pathway linked to the experiment that supports it. The collection also links to computational models so that a researcher can compare an experimental finding with the assumptions used to represent it. This work forms part of the AARL's NeuroNex Communication, Coordination, and Control in Nervous Systems (C3NS) effort.
passages.judgment: Names the nerve, response, preparation, and modeling choice that make a source-linked collection necessary.

passages.author: Reader reproducing the lookup
passages.question: Which app can I open?
passages.before: The primary deliverable is SADb Explorer, a browser application containing 1,393 literature and related records. It has four main tabs (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}, callout~(A)): Table searches individual records, Pivot compares classifications, Bubble map explores citation links among papers, and Search (online) finds candidate additions through OpenAlex, an open bibliographic index. The records, notes, and citation graph are embedded in the application, so the first three tabs can be used without an internet connection. Search (online) requires an internet connection and lets the user save candidate records for later curation. The application preserves both the records retained for active curation and archived records from the collected material.
passages.after: Open SADb Explorer in a browser using \path{SADb_audit/app/sadb_app.html} in the project repository. Three tabs work offline (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}A). Table retrieves individual records, Pivot counts papers that share classifications, and Bubble map follows citations. Search (online) queries the OpenAlex bibliographic index for candidates to save for later curation.\par
passages.judgment: The tracked expanded app contains all 1,393 records and exposes the record and archive filters. The dist version only exposes 943 Papers.

passages.author: Database reviewer
passages.question: Which papers belong to the citation graph?
passages.before: Within the application's Papers category, containing 943 entries, 833 carry curation notes, 606 have tags for the animals or human participants studied, 316 carry animal-study assessments, 119 link to feedback pathways, 95 carry an afferent classification, and 363 carry robot-or-simulation translation notes. DOI identifiers are present for 892 papers, and 318 have attached-PDF indicators. Within the Papers category, 730 papers are connected by 11,130 directed citation pairs. The Louvain algorithm identifies citation communities: groups of papers with comparatively dense citation connections. The application labels these communities as 18 named topic clusters (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}, callout~(G)), which help users navigate related studies in the Bubble map tab.
passages.after: Within the application's Papers category, containing 943 entries, 833 carry curation notes, 606 have tags for the animals or human participants studied, 316 carry animal-study assessments, 119 link to feedback pathways, 95 carry an afferent classification, and 363 carry robot-or-simulation translation notes. DOI identifiers are present for 892 papers, and 318 have attached-PDF indicators. Of these Papers, 730 cite at least one other Paper in the collection. Counting both citing and cited papers gives 816 distinct Papers connected by 11,130 directed citation pairs. The Louvain algorithm identifies groups of papers with relatively dense citation links. The application labels these communities as 18 named topic clusters (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}, callout~(G)), which help users navigate related studies in the Bubble map tab.
passages.judgment: 730 is the count of papers with outgoing citations. The union of citing and cited endpoints is 816. The edge count of 11,130 and the 18 communities are unchanged.

passages.author: Ben and independent reader
passages.question: Can I follow a pathway record back to a study?
passages.before: The Table tab combines text search with filters for animal or human study category, pathway, afferent class, record type, archive status, year, and note or PDF availability (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_explorer}). Selecting a record opens its source information, curation notes, and notes on how the reported findings could inform a robot or simulation. The Search (online) tab queries OpenAlex for candidate additions and marks DOIs already represented in SADb.
passages.after: The Table tab retrieves both a paper and the evidence recorded for it. For example, choosing \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} in the \emph{Pathway} filter returns six Papers (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_explorer}). Select the row for \citet{mccrea_disynaptic_1995} to open its record. The drawer shows the source DOI, the Cat classification, both Ia and Ib afferent tags, and two pathway labels, \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} and \emph{Ib disynaptic inhibition}. Reading the experiment explains why both labels apply.
passages.judgment: The actual Table search returns six Papers. The item for McCrea et al. links to its DOI and displays Cat, Ia, Ib, and both pathway names. Enlarged genuine screen regions replace the Deng screenshot.

passages.author: Primary experiment and independent reader
passages.question: What can a modeler take from the experiment?
passages.before: For example, a researcher may ask whether type Ia feedback excites the muscle from which it originates or inhibits its antagonist. SADb contains separate pathway records for ``Ia monosynaptic excitation'' and ``Ia inhibitory.'' These describe complementary connections: direct excitation of the agonist motor pool and inhibition of an antagonist through an inhibitory interneuron. The researcher can inspect the linked studies and model records to compare their target muscles, intervening neurons, and task conditions before choosing how to implement the sensory afferent pathways. The afferent class alone does not specify the sign of every connection.\par
passages.after: In decerebrate cats at rest, stimulating the plantaris nerve at group~I strength inhibited medial gastrocnemius motor neurons. With the same stimulus during extension in midbrain-evoked fictive locomotion, the recorded response was excitatory. In this preparation the neural rhythm was present while the animal was immobilized. Nerve stimulation recruited group~I fibers and did not isolate Ib fibers.
passages.judgment: The same group I nerve stimulus inhibited the synergist motor pool at rest and excited it during extension in midbrain-evoked fictive locomotion. A signed diagram conveys the net response without assigning unmeasured interneurons or gains.

passages.author: Ben and database reviewer
passages.question: Will a reader understand the app?
passages.before: The Pivot tab counts papers by two selected dimensions, including topic cluster, decade, primary author, animal or human study category, feedback pathway, and afferent classification. Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_pivot} crosses afferent classes with categories of animal and human studies: each cell counts papers carrying both tags. Rows and columns can be ordered alphabetically or by count. Selecting a cell opens the corresponding records in the Table tab, and a return control restores the pivot. The pivot is computed over the 943 entries in the Papers category, including archived entries, rather than all 1,393 records. Because a paper can carry several animal or afferent tags, it can contribute to several cells. The counts describe the distribution of curated records, not independent experimental observations or the strength of evidence for a pathway.
passages.after: Pivot answers a different question. With the Table filters cleared, choose \emph{Afferent types} and \emph{Animal}, then select the Ib--Cat cell (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_pivot}). Table opens the 21 Papers counted in that cell. \emph{Back to pivot} restores the comparison. A paper can carry more than one afferent or animal tag and appear in several cells. A cell count consequently describes how much material a researcher can inspect for a particular combination.
passages.judgment: The Ib and Cat cell counts 21 Papers. Selecting it opens the contributing rows. The screenshot also shows the return control. The worked Table, Pivot, and Bubble map tasks follow one another.

passages.author: Database reviewer
passages.question: What does the map count and which control changes it?
passages.before: Selecting a paper makes it the reference for the displayed citation neighborhood; the application calls this the focus paper. Its source information appears in the left record area (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}, callout~(C)), together with its curation note and notes on possible applications to a robot or simulation (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}, callout~(D)). The neighborhood selector displays papers up to one, two, or three citation links from the focus paper, following either its references or papers that cite it (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}, callout~(E)). A two-link neighborhood adds one level beyond the directly connected papers. Directly connected papers retain color, while papers reached through additional links are gray. In the illustrated neighborhood of the Grillner (1985) focus paper, 57 in-corpus papers cite it, it cites 13 in-corpus papers, and 555 papers lie within two links. Green triangles identify papers that cite the focus paper, and red circles identify papers cited by it.
passages.after: Selecting a paper makes it the reference for the displayed citation neighborhood; the application calls this the focus paper. Its source information appears in the left record area (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}, callout~(C)), together with its curation note and notes on possible applications to a robot or simulation (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}, callout~(D)). The neighborhood selector in callout~(B) displays papers up to one, two, or three citation links from the focus paper. Callout~(E) marks the resulting neighborhood, which includes both references and citing papers. A two-link neighborhood adds one level beyond the directly connected papers. Directly connected papers retain color, while papers reached through additional links are gray. In the illustrated neighborhood of the Grillner (1985) focus paper, 57 in-corpus papers cite it, it cites 13 in-corpus papers, and the two-link display contains 555 papers including the focus paper itself. Green triangles identify papers that cite the focus paper, and red circles identify papers cited by it.
passages.judgment: B changes depth and E marks the resulting neighborhood. The 555 displayed Papers include the focus record and 554 other Papers.

passages.author: Ben and technical reader
passages.question: Which graphical tool changes a runnable circuit?
passages.before: In the graphical editor, a researcher can place nonspiking neurons, draw synapses between them, inspect a synapse's strength and reversal potential, and save the circuit. The Build action generates a Simulink circuit from that saved description. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_signal_contracts} gives the editor command and build script. The knee and arm examples use separate builders to add their actuator, sensory, and mechanical blocks.
passages.after: In the SNS-Simscape interface, \texttt{SNSGui}, a researcher can place nonspiking neurons, connect them with synapses, inspect a synapse's strength and reversal potential, and save the circuit. Choosing \emph{Build} generates the neural portion of a Simulink model. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_signal_contracts} gives the command and build script. Separate builders connect the knee and arm circuits to their actuators, sensory inputs, and mechanical models.
passages.judgment: SNSGui builds a nonspiking Simulink circuit. The knee and arm builders add the mechanics. The separate drawing tool is absent from Chapter 6.

passages.author: Defense-folder audit
passages.question: What did the fitting tool vary?
passages.before: The search scripts bound the parameters, tie corresponding left and right values when symmetry is intended, and use tree-structured Parzen estimation to select candidates from earlier scores. They save the parameters, components of the score, and reason each trial ended. A selected candidate is rerun in a fresh process before any intervention.
passages.after: For rhythm and sensory timing, the search scripts use tree-structured Parzen estimation to propose new parameter sets from earlier scores. For the s3k and syn6 controllers, a separate bounded least-squares fit adjusts the connections from pattern-formation channels to motor neurons to match the reference muscle recruitment. Corresponding weights are tied across sides when the fit calls for symmetry. The physical test then loads the saved settings, records the components of its score and the reason the trial ended, and repeats a selected trial in a fresh process before an intervention.
passages.judgment: TPE proposes rhythm and timing parameters. Bounded least squares fits pattern-formation to motor-neuron weights in s3k and syn6.

passages.author: Defense-folder audit
passages.question: What can I recover from a completed trial?
passages.before: In a pathway-removal experiment, the unaffected controller parameters, drive, support, and external force protocol stay fixed. In a stimulation experiment, the driver changes the injected current at one location and repeats the trial from the same state. Aligning RG, PF, and MN voltages with joint motion, actuator force, and support force identifies where the responses first diverge.
passages.after: In a pathway-removal experiment, the unaffected controller parameters, drive, support, and external force stay fixed. For a stimulation experiment, the driver changes the injected current at one location and repeats the trial from the same state. For the Gait2392 trials, I developed a recorder that saves the timing of neural inputs and updates alongside joint states, muscle commands, foot loads, and harness forces. A researcher can align the signals at the stimulus or foot-contact event and locate the first response that differs. The saved joint states also allow the movement to be viewed again without running the controller a second time.
passages.judgment: Saved timestamps align neural and mechanical signals. Reloading the saved poses reproduces the observed motion.

passages.author: Ben and source profiles
passages.question: Whose model, and which configuration?
passages.before: In the second timing test, Hunt-PT+RC used a Peterka--Ting-inspired balance pathway (PT) that responds to motion of the model's center of mass. Its Renshaw cells (RC) receive motor-neuron input and feed inhibition back to the same motor pool. I compared sparse execution with a compact version that reuses working arrays and calculates ionic current only for channels with nonzero conductance.
passages.after: The second timing test used a 1,033-cell configuration with a Peterka--Ting-inspired balance pathway that responds to motion of the model's center of mass. Its Renshaw cells receive motor-neuron input and feed inhibition back to the same motor pool. I compared sparse execution with a compact version that reuses working arrays and calculates ionic current only for channels with nonzero conductance.
passages.judgment: BiW2Lvar+ identifies Ben's controller family. The timed configurations are identified by neuron count, balance feedback, and Renshaw inhibition. The configuration for the reported suspended test is distinct.

passages.author: Ben and Overleaf author capture
passages.question: What happened in suspension and on release?
passages.before: For an earlier course project, I built a neuromechanical model in AnimatLab and worked with Morrow to couple the Deng circuit to the Li walker and tune it by hand. The legs performed stepping-like motion while it was suspended in air. However, but the model fell over when lowered to the ground and support was removed. I developed the tools in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} to trace the consequences of a controller or mechanical change from neural activity to muscle force and joint motion. For example, an extensor sensory pulse extended the simulated knee. In a supported walker, removing selected sensory inputs changed the timing of footfalls even though the body continued to move forward. Recording both contact and movement exposed the coordination deficit.
passages.after: For an earlier course project, I built a neuromechanical model in AnimatLab and worked with Morrow to couple the Deng circuit to the Li walker and tune it by hand. The legs performed stepping-like motion while it was suspended in air. However, the model fell over when lowered to the ground and support was removed. I developed the tools in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} to trace the consequences of a controller or mechanical change from neural activity to muscle force and joint motion. For example, an extensor sensory pulse extended the simulated knee. In a supported walker, removing selected sensory inputs changed the timing of footfalls even though the body continued to move forward. Recording both contact and movement exposed the coordination deficit.
passages.judgment: Retains Ben's observed stepping-like motion in air and fall on removal of support. Removed the repeated conjunction from the live edit.

passages.author: Ben and archive
passages.question: Where is the original FEA illustration?
passages.before: \caption[End deformation and proposed BPA experiments]{Proposed investigation of the end effect. (A) The fittings constrain the local diameter while the central span expands. The profiles show the geometric hypothesis. (B) An axial guide permits free or loaded shortening, while locking the guide gives an isometric force test. Diameter and fitting separation distinguish wall deformation from fitting motion.}

The separated surfaces identify the rubber wall, two oppositely wound aramid fiber families, and the outer covering. passages.author: Ben and curation evaluation
passages.question: What has to change for assisted classification to be viable?
passages.before: The monthly literature watch supplies candidates for manual curation (Section~\ref{sec:sadb_methods}). For a pathway such as extensor group~I excitation, the most useful addition to a record would be a direct link from each reported sign to its preparation, stimulus, and phase. A reader could then distinguish a measured reversal from an assumption in a computational model before following their citation links. The Bubble map already identifies citation communities by color. Grouping their papers spatially would provide a second way to locate related studies \citep{bolen_using_2024}.
passages.after: Future researchers can revisit large language models for classification as the tools improve. In our earlier evaluation, finding related papers was more successful than assigning them to the right categories \citep{bolen_using_2024}. A model could propose a pathway label and identify the passage that supports it. A researcher would read the experiment and approve, correct, or reject the label before it enters SADb. \citet{chomsky_false_promise_2023} distinguish predicting plausible text from explaining why a conclusion follows. In the McCrea example, the words \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} alone do not tell a curator which fibers were stimulated. Comparing suggested labels with independently curated records, and measuring the time required to check them, would show whether newer models help with that work.
passages.judgment: Propose source-grounded labels, an independent curation comparison, and a human decision. The Chomsky, Roberts, and Watumull guest essay is an argument about explanation. The empirical test uses the project's screening experience.

passages.author: Ben and technical reader
passages.question: Can the current drawing change what runs?
passages.before: Future researchers can test whether particular sensory inputs contribute to the extra bursts in the third pattern-formation channel during movement. The suspended six-synergy trial provides a record of the extra bursts and the joint motion at their onset. Replaying the same recorded motion while changing one sensory pathway at a time can distinguish the effect of that pathway from the accompanying change in knee angle. The layer-specific stimuli already tested in a reduced circuit can then be applied to the six-synergy controller under load. Stimulating the rhythm generator, a pattern-formation channel, or a motor neuron in separate trials can distinguish a reset of the rhythm from a missing motor burst with preserved phase (Section~\ref{sec:app_layer_stimulus}). Published responses provide a reference for those interventions \citep{selionov_tonic_2009,rybak_modelling_2006,markin_afferent_2010,shevtsova_modeling_2016}.
passages.after: Future researchers can develop an application that links a connectome drawing to the controller used in a simulation. A researcher could select a sensory connection in the drawing, change its strength in the controller, and rerun a saved experiment with the same mechanical model, stimulus, and support. Reproducing the result of the same change made directly in the controller would test that the application updated the intended synapse.
passages.judgment: A diagram-to-simulator application is future work. A direct change in the controller gives a reference for testing the proposed application.

passages.author: Ben and defense source
passages.question: Which comparison does the slide suggest for a manuscript?
passages.before: No equivalent Chapter 7 figure in the captured manuscript.
passages.after: Figure~\ref{fig:discussion_neuromechanical_workflow} shows how to locate the first change in coordination. To test a sensory pathway, repeat the stimulus with the body, drive, and support held fixed. To test an actuator route, keep the controller fixed. A force shortfall at a known pressure points to the actuator or its route. If force is adequate but the foot accepts load late, compare when the muscle was recruited and when the joint moved.
passages.judgment: The new portrait Figure 7.5 takes one baseline into two alternative controlled repeats and identifies the signals to compare. Chapter 7.3 supplies the interpretation.

The graphical editor covers circuit wiring. The preparation, parameter searches, and replay have model-specific script entry points. For the newer coupled experiments, the available records vary by test. The noise and pulse runs include the applied currents and aligned states. passages.author: Ben and independent reader
passages.question: What does Appendix E add?
passages.before: Of the 561 retained Papers, 523 have curation notes, 426 have preparation tags, 240 have an animal-study assessment, and 118 link to at least one named feedback pathway. Afferent classes are recorded for 86 Papers, robot or simulation translation notes for 258, and a DOI for 550. A paper can contribute to several of these counts.
passages.after: Of the 561 retained Papers, 523 have curation notes, 426 have an animal or human study tag, 240 have an animal-study assessment, and 118 link to at least one named feedback pathway. Afferent classes are recorded for 86 Papers, robot or simulation translation notes for 258, and a DOI for 550. A paper can contribute to several of these counts.
passages.judgment: Distinguishes 957 maintained from 436 archived, and overlapping classifications from unique records. The 426 records have animal or human tags, not preparation tags. Tables E1 and E2 give receptors, possible inputs, and eight named pathways.

passages.author: Primary experiment and independent reader
passages.question: What alternative condition matters to a specialist?
passages.before: Table~\ref{tab:sadb_afferents} relates each receptor to a candidate model input. Table~\ref{tab:sadb_pathways} gives the pathway names as they appear in the database. In the Table view, the \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} pathway filter returns six Papers. The record for \citet{mccrea_disynaptic_1995} carries both Ia and Ib tags and links to both \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} and \emph{Ib disynaptic inhibition}. Chapter~\ref{ch:overall} compares the experimental conditions behind those two links.
passages.after: Table~\ref{tab:sadb_afferents} relates each receptor to a candidate model input, and Table~\ref{tab:sadb_pathways} gives the searchable pathway names. The two pathway links in the McCrea record illustrate why the preparation belongs alongside the label (Section~\ref{sec:sadb_worked_rule}). In the acute spinal preparation treated with clonidine, the inhibition seen at rest diminished during fictive locomotion, but the short-latency excitation seen in the midbrain-evoked preparation did not appear \citep{mccrea_disynaptic_1995}. A model of the spinal preparation would therefore need a different test from the one drawn in Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_group_i_rule}. The Ib pathway label is a way to retrieve this paper. Its Ia and Ib afferent tags preserve the broader identity of the stimulated group~I fibers.
passages.judgment: In the clonidine-treated acute spinal preparation, inhibition diminished and the short-latency excitation was absent. A model of that preparation requires a different test.

passages.author: Ben, advisor comment, and independent reader
passages.question: What questions required new tools and a robot-specific model?
passages.before: I developed the tools in this chapter to couple neural controllers to Gait2392, a human musculoskeletal model, and to mechanical models based on the computer-aided design (CAD) of our bipedal robot. Slow simulation and hand tuning in an earlier course project with Connor Morrow made it difficult to repeat the same experiment after changing the controller or the mechanical model. A scripted version of the walker in the MuJoCo physics engine made automatic tuning possible. The subsequent experiments use the human model, a robot counterpart with relocated muscle paths, and a model built from the lab robot's own geometry. I developed Simulink blocks and a graphical interface for building nonspiking circuits. A simulated knee reflex tests whether a sensory signal passes through a motor neuron and muscle to produce joint motion. The final experiments use scripts to tune controllers, test whether the feet alternate under load, and measure how much a faster neural calculation saves over a complete trial.
passages.after: This chapter presents the tools I developed to test neural controllers on a human musculoskeletal model and on models of our bipedal robot. The lab's existing software made it impractical to search systematically for controller settings. The human model provided a reference for movement, but testing the robot required a model that represented where its artificial muscles pulled on the joints and how the resulting motion fed back to the controller. I built tools to construct circuits graphically, connect controllers to these mechanical models, and automate tuning. Researchers can now change a sensory connection or move an artificial muscle attachment in simulation, repeat the trial under the same conditions, and trace the effect on muscle force and leg motion.
passages.judgment: The lab needed systematic controller tuning and models that could return feedback from the motion produced by the robot's own muscle paths and joints. Changing one connection or attachment and repeating the trial reveals its effect on muscle force and leg motion.
passages.disposition_of_previous_judgment: Reopened. The earlier review scored the paragraphs separately and missed that the first section restarted the overview.
passages.advisor_comment: It is like you are starting the previous paragraph all over again. These should be combined into a single paragraph. I don't think all these details on the neural model are helpful as it introduces a large stream of terms the reader doesn't know anything about at this time.
passages.advisor_anchor: For a course project in neuromechanical modeling

passages.author: Ben, advisor comment, and independent reader
passages.question: Which earlier experiment exposed the limitation?
passages.before: I built my first neuromechanical model in AnimatLab, a graphical program in which a neural circuit can activate muscles and receive sensory signals from the moving body \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. For the course project, Morrow and I connected the circuit of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} to the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} and adjusted neural currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand. The circuit supplied a common rhythm to both legs, and opposing muscles pulled on each limb. There is a passive toe joint. The legs made stepping-like movements while the model was suspended in air. When we lowered it to the ground and removed the support, the model fell over (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}). Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Each parameter change required another slow run, making a systematic search impractical.
passages.after: In a course project, Connor Morrow and I tested whether the neural circuit of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} could coordinate the legs of the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017}. We connected the circuit and body in AnimatLab, a graphical program for linking neurons, muscles, and sensory feedback \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}, and adjusted neural currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand. The circuit supplied a common rhythm to both legs, and opposing muscles pulled on each limb. There is a passive toe joint. The legs made stepping-like movements while the model was suspended in air. When we lowered it to the ground and removed the support, the model fell over (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}). Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Each parameter change required another slow run.
passages.judgment: Morrow and Bolen tested the published Deng circuit on the Li biped. The legs made stepping-like movements in suspension, the model fell when support was removed, and each parameter change cost another slow run. This is the reader's first account of the course project.
passages.disposition_of_previous_judgment: Reopened. The earlier review scored the paragraphs separately and missed that the first section restarted the overview.
passages.advisor_comment: It is like you are starting the previous paragraph all over again. These should be combined into a single paragraph. I don't think all these details on the neural model are helpful as it introduces a large stream of terms the reader doesn't know anything about at this time.
passages.advisor_anchor: For a course project in neuromechanical modeling
